An online mathematical encyclopedia devoted to Deriving and exploring mathematics beyond the classroom for high school students. All Things Are Derivable

Our mission is to make mathematical reasoning transparent, tangible, and telling through Derivation while offering additional pathways for inquisitive and motivated students to explore mathematics with greter rigor and depth.
This project aims to demystify mathematical Deriving and to foster deeper curiosity through clear and careful reasoning.

Throughout this project, Derivation is treated as a proper noun, referring to the process of obtain a result through meticulous, step-by-step calculation. As the main theme of Art of Derivation, all words related to Derivation (such as Derive, Deriving) are highlighted in the main theme color. Some closely related terms, though not strictly equivalent, including Proof, Justification, and Logical Argument, all of which are integral to the idea of Derivation presented in this project. My understanding of Derivation was mainly developed from my AP Physics C: Mechanics course, where the Free Response Questions frequently require student to Derive expressions from fundamental definitions or equations in the provided equations sheet.
This project is built on Docusaurus and deployed on GitHub Pages. Below are detailed format information.

All documents start with the front matter to ensure the consistent format and navigation. More additional details, refer to Markdown Features | Docusaurus.

In everyday life we constantly reduce and simplify things, and that idea is the central theme of this course. Example Stories: reduce the human condition Fables/Myths: reduce morality Law: reduces justice GPA: reduces "you" The problem with reduction is that it always leaves something out. It therefore has to be done with care: we must decide deliberately what to leave out and what to keep. Probability and Statistics are tools for making sense of data and using it to make decisions. They give us quantitative ways to study reduction. Goals Our goals as they pertain to data reduction: Examine the different types of data reduction Develop effective ways to visualize and communicate data Quantify our expectations for the data — this is Probability Draw inferences and conclusions from the data — this is Statistics Recognize several common fallacies that can knock us off course

Logical Fallacy A Logical Fallacy occurs when rules of inference are erroneously used, or incorrect ones are invoked. A fallacy indicates faulty — wrong — reasoning, even if the inferred conclusion happens to be true.

Data Visualization is a form of Qualitative Reduction, and there is rarely one correct answer to a problem. Every effective Data Visualization has a Message, and there are ways to deliver that message more clearly, such as: Add a title Add annotations Choose an intuitive graph type Characteristics of a Good Data Visualization Characteristics Description Clear The message is easy to grasp at a glance, with no clutter or ambiguity Concise Shows only what is needed to carry the message, with no extra decoration or data Concrete Uses specific values, units, and real quantities rather than vague or abstract shapes Contextual Supplies what is needed to interpret it, such as labels, scale, units, reference points, and the data source Correct Represents the data accurately and without distortion (honest axes, proportions, comparisons) There are four types of message, and each has its own favored graphs: Types of Message Comparison Bar Chart Radar Chart Line Plot Ridgeline Plot Composition Pie Chart Stacked Bar Chart Unit Plot Stacked Area Chart Distribution Bar Histogram Line Histogram Jitter Plot Box Plot Relation Heat Map Scatter Plot Point Cloud Plot Quantile-Quantile Plot

Fundamental Principle of Counting Suppose nnn decisions are made in sequence, where at the iiith step there are kik_iki​ available options. If each decision is made independently (meaning the outcome of one will not influence or be influenced by any other), then the total number of unique ways to perform all nnn decisions is ∏i=1nki=k1×k2×⋯×kn\prod_{i=1}^{n}k_{i}=k_1\times k_2\times \cdots \times k_ni=1∏n​ki​=k1​×k2​×⋯×kn​

There are four counting methods, depending on two questions: does order matter? And can choices repeat? When order matters, we call it Permutations; on the contrary, when order does not matters, we call it Combinations. When choices can repeat, we say the selection is with Replacement; on the contrary, when choices cannot repeat, we call it without Replacement.
